title: Virtual Ion-Optics Testbed (VIOT)
description: A multiscale assessment of carbon-nanomaterial accelerator-grid coatings for charge-exchange erosion mitigation in the NASA NSTAR ion thruster — GPU PIC-MCC plasma simulation, LAMMPS AIREBO molecular dynamics, and custom 3D Poisson/DSMC solvers.

title: Time-Series Modeling of Pulsed-Mode N₂O RCS Thrusters
description: A five-phase computational study for ICAETM 2026: a lumped-parameter physics model of catalytic N₂O decomposition, statistical characterization of the resulting pulse-train time series, and an LSTM predictive model benchmarked against an ARIMA baseline.

detail.tagline: A lumped-parameter physics model of a pulsed nitrous-oxide monopropellant thruster, turned into a time series, characterized statistically, and forecast with an LSTM.
overview: Pulsed-mode N₂O monopropellant reaction-control thrusters fire in short duty-cycle bursts, and each pulse leaves thermal state (catalyst-bed temperature, chamber soak-back) behind for the next one. This project builds a lumped-parameter physics model of catalytic N₂O decomposition, drives it through a realistic pulse-train duty cycle, and treats the resulting per-pulse impulse-bit / chamber / bed measurements as a time series rather than a set of independent samples.

The pipeline is five layers deep: a physics model of a single pulse, a pulse-train generator that carries thermal state forward between pulses (soak-back), a statistical characterization pass (drift, periodicity, stationarity), predictive models benchmarked against a classical baseline, and a six-figure, paper-quality visualization suite.

pipeline.body: Real parameter ranges for N₂O monopropellant thrusters, encoded as defaults in config.py.
Lumped-parameter single-pulse model of chamber pressure, chamber temperature, and catalyst-bed temperature.
A duty-cycle engine fires a pulse train and carries thermal state forward between pulses (soak-back), producing 600 lognormal-spaced and 400 uniform-spaced pulse datasets.
Drift, Mann-Kendall trend test, Augmented Dickey-Fuller stationarity, autocorrelation, and FFT spectral analysis on every feature.
An LSTM forecaster evaluated out-of-sample against a classical ARIMA(1,0,1) baseline on RMSE/MAE.
16 paper-quality figures (PNG @300 DPI + matching SVG) plus a graphical abstract and animations.

resultsTable2.caption: LSTM vs. ARIMA(1,0,1) out-of-sample forecast error

chart.caption: LSTM's RMSE improvement over the ARIMA(1,0,1) baseline

findings: Bed start temperature is where the LSTM earns its keep — 61.1% RMSE improvement over ARIMA, because soak-back drift between pulses is a nonlinear, state-dependent effect a linear ARIMA model can't capture.
Mean thrust and peak chamber pressure are only mildly improved by the LSTM (4.9–7.8%) — these are closer to stationary, weakly-drifting series where ARIMA is already competitive.

All four characterized features are stationary in levels (ADF), and three of four show a statistically significant increasing drift (Mann-Kendall p = 0.0) — consistent with progressive catalyst-bed thermal loading across a 600-pulse duty cycle.
Every dataset, table, and figure in the repo is regenerable from the analysis/ CLI suite with a fixed random seed.

title: Tensor Basis Neural Networks vs. Random Forests for RANS Turbulence Closure
description: A methods study for ICMAI-MAC 2026 (NIT Goa) comparing Tensor Basis Neural Networks and Tensor Basis Random Forests as machine-learned Reynolds-stress anisotropy closures on the NASA wall-mounted hump benchmark, with spatially-resolved SHAP analysis.

detail.tagline: Two machine-learned RANS turbulence closures, trained on periodic hills and tested — out of distribution — on a NASA benchmark, explained with SHAP.
overview: The Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations are unclosed: they require a model for the Reynolds-stress anisotropy tensor. Pope's (1975) tensor-basis formulation writes that tensor as a linear combination of ten invariant basis functions, with the combination weights left as scalar functions of five flow-state invariants — exactly the shape a Tensor Basis Neural Network (Ling et al., 2016) or Tensor Basis Random Forest (Kaandorp & Dwight, 2020) can learn.

This thesis trains both architectures with a matched 50-trial Bayesian-optimization budget and a 5-seed protocol, exclusively on a family of flow over periodic hills (PHLL29), then evaluates both — without any retraining — on the held-out, out-of-distribution NASA wall-mounted hump (NASAHUMP) benchmark. The central methodological contribution is a spatially- and state-resolved SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) attribution of each model's closure decision, projected onto both the classical Lumley barycentric triangle and the Wnek et al. (2025) polar invariant map.

chart.caption: RMSE: in-distribution validation vs. out-of-distribution NASAHUMP test

dataset.label: NASAHUMP
dataset.value: Held-out OOD test — NASA wall-mounted hump

findings: The two architectures invert their ordering between validation and generalization: TBNN wins in-distribution, but TBRF is clearly superior out-of-distribution (signed-rank test across 5 seeds, p = 0.0). The random forest's depth-limited, bootstrap-averaged structure acts as an inductive bias against the aggressive extrapolation neural networks perform off-manifold.

TBRF never violates the Lumley-triangle realizability bounds — its piecewise-constant, convex-combination output can never leave the convex hull of physically admissible training states. TBNN violates realizability on ~1.19% of test points, concentrated in the separation bubble where extrapolation is most aggressive.
TBNN is also the only model with meaningful cross-seed variance (concentrated in the recirculation region); TBRF is statistically near-deterministic (cross-seed RMSE std 6.7×10⁻⁵).

SHAP attribution shows the two models are locally attending to different physical mechanisms: TBRF concentrates on invariants I1/I2 (strain and rotation magnitude) at the separation bubble, while TBNN spreads weight onto the higher-order I3–I5 invariants with a fatter attribution tail — and the TBNN's error hot-spots co-locate almost exactly with where its SHAP attribution diverges from TBRF's.
26-figure publication-quality graphical catalog (30 rendered panels), full metric tables, and per-figure interpretation are documented in the thesis.

title: Smart Ambulance Device-Interoperability Gateway
description: A working connected-ambulance prototype: auto-detects BLE medical-device protocols, prioritizes vital-sign data under bandwidth loss, stores-and-forwards offline, and normalizes telemetry into FHIR-style JSON for a hospital triage dashboard.

detail.tagline: An ESP32 edge gateway that auto-detects medical-device protocols with zero manual configuration, and decides what survives a bandwidth drop.
overview: Built for an Indian engineering PBL course (ME305, Pune Vidyarthi Griha COE) around a patent-oriented claim: auto-detecting a connected medical device's protocol without manual configuration, and prioritizing which data streams survive a bandwidth drop. The system has three clearly separated interfaces — a laptop-side Project Command Center for creating patients and injecting clinical/network scenarios, background Python simulators that generate realistic BLE GATT telemetry for three real Health Device Profiles, and a Hospital Triage Dashboard served either from the ESP32 itself or locally.

The ESP32 parses `GATT_SVC:<uuid>` discovery lines and fixed-size binary frames over TCP or USB serial, normalizes readings into FHIR-style JSON observations with real LOINC codes, and applies offline-resilient store-and-forward with bandwidth-adaptive prioritization: waveform data drops first, then vitals, alerts survive last.

architecture.detail: Real BLE GATT profiles: Heart Rate (0x180D), Pulse Oximeter (0x1822), Blood Pressure (0x1810).
ESP32 firmware + a Python software mirror, both parsing the same wire protocol.
Maps raw readings to observations with real LOINC codes (8867-4, 59408-5, 8480-6, 8462-4, 9279-1) and evaluates alert thresholds.
Priority queue drops waveform → vitals → alert in that order when full; "transmits" via a logged TX event with a 5% simulated failure rate.
Two renderings: embedded HTML served directly from the ESP32, and a FastAPI-rendered local copy.

findings: A full end-to-end demo was verified on 2026-08-29: a patient created in the Command Center → simulators streamed live GATT telemetry over the LAN → the ESP32 parsed, normalized, and evaluated alerts → the dashboard reflected live values, with an injected tachycardia scenario correctly flashing a critical alert.
The ESP32 firmware includes a hand-rolled captive-portal Wi-Fi provisioning flow: it joins a saved network on boot, or falls back to its own access point with a `/setup` page.

The one gap from a production system: transmission to a hospital backend is currently simulated (a logged TX event), not a real HTTP egress — everything upstream of that (detection, parsing, normalization, prioritization, dashboard) runs on real hardware.

title: Chandrayaan-2 OHRC Lunar Imagery Toolkit
description: A Smart India Hackathon entry (SIH26166) building image co-registration, calibration, and matching tools for Chandrayaan-2 Orbiter High Resolution Camera (OHRC) lunar surface imagery from ISRO's PRADAN archive.

detail.tagline: Pixel-accurate correspondence across three lunar imaging payloads that never see the Moon the same way — 20–300× scale gaps, shifting shadows, near-featureless terrain.
overview: Chandrayaan-2's orbiter carries three optical payloads that are almost impossible to directly compare: OHRC (~0.25–0.3 m/px, narrow 3 km strips), TMC-2 (5 m/px, near-global stereo triplets), and IIRS (~80 m/px, 250+ band hyperspectral). SIH26166 asks for pixel-accurate correspondence between them despite 20–300× scale differences, sun-angle-dependent shadow shifts (acute near the lunar south pole, where Sun elevation is often under 5°), and lunar terrain so texturally repetitive that naive keypoint matchers produce false positives at scale.

The toolkit builds a feature-matching pipeline (SIFT and AKAZE, with CLAHE and gradient-magnitude preprocessing variants, an 8-way dihedral transform search, and RANSAC affine estimation) and validates it two ways before trusting it on real data: a synthetic ground-truth test that warps a strip by a known random affine transform and checks recovery within tolerance, and a negative control that confirms two non-overlapping crops of the same strip do not falsely match.

dataset.label: 4 product IDs
dataset.value: Real OHRC passes from ISRO's PRADAN archive

dataset.label: ~0.25–0.3 m/px
dataset.value: OHRC native resolution, ~3 km strip swath
Scale gap spanned across OHRC / TMC-2 / IIRS

findings: Real OHRC pass pairs were pulled from ISRO's PRADAN archive (four product IDs spanning different acquisition passes) to stress-test the matcher against genuine sun-angle and cross-pass variation, not just synthetic warps.

A dedicated experiment battery searches the matcher-configuration space (raw / CLAHE / gradient-magnitude preprocessing × SIFT / AKAZE × dihedral orientation search) to find which configuration survives real cross-pass sun-angle pairs, rather than assuming one setting works everywhere.

The validation harness explicitly separates two different failure modes that matter for a hackathon judge: recoverability (does the matcher find the right known transform?) and specificity (does it correctly refuse to match unrelated crops?) — both are required for a registration tool to be trustworthy on sparse, ambiguous lunar imagery.

title: AeroSpace Multiphysics Pipeline
description: A GPU-accelerated multiphysics pipeline for NSTAR ion thruster plasma simulation — charge-exchange kinetics through WarpX PIC to Fowler–Nordheim field-emission risk assessment, comparing Molybdenum against GNP coatings.
status: Physics + orchestration implemented — GPU PIC runs pending

detail.tagline: A five-stage GPU pipeline chaining charge-exchange kinetics to a full WarpX Particle-in-Cell simulation of the NSTAR gridded ion thruster, tuned to survive an 8 GB laptop GPU.
overview: NSTAR's accelerator grid is bombarded by slow charge-exchange (CEX) ions born inside its own accelerating field. This pipeline chains five physics stages — Rapp-Francis CEX and Lotz ionisation cross sections, plasma parameter estimation (Debye length, plasma frequency), a Monte Carlo Collision pre-flight beam-loss estimate to sanity-check settings before committing GPU time, a full WarpX GPU Particle-in-Cell simulation, and a Fowler-Nordheim field-emission risk atlas — to compare a baseline Molybdenum accelerator grid against a Graphene Nanoplatelet (GNP) coating.

The whole pipeline is tuned around one hard constraint: an 8 GB RTX 4060 laptop GPU. Getting WarpX to not OOM-kill on that budget required deliberate departures from the stock configuration — documented as a before/after table so the reasoning survives the next person who touches it.

resultsTable.caption: GPU-memory fixes for an 8 GB RTX 4060 (vs. stock WarpX defaults)
rows: Esirkepov on a periodic grid needs 602×602 guard cells → OOM; direct keeps guard cells at 2×2
Both dimensions divisible by 32 for CUDA warp-aligned, coalesced memory access
Explicitly reserves 6 of 8 GB VRAM, leaving 2 GB headroom
Dropping the current-density field halves diagnostic write memory
Disabling the field smoother saves roughly 100 MB

resultsTable2.caption: Baseline Molybdenum vs. GNP-coated accelerator grid (config/nstar_base.yaml)

findings: Kinetics, plasma-parameter, and Fowler-Nordheim atlas math are implemented and unit-tested (three Windows-safe test suites covering cross sections, MCC beam-loss estimate, and PICMI-config translation) — all runnable without a GPU or WSL2.
The full GPU PIC production run requires WSL2 with a CUDA-enabled WarpX build; a one-shot setup script and a documented `.wslconfig` (12 GB RAM, 8 processors, 4 GB swap) make that reproducible.

The GNP coating's 200× higher field-enhancement factor is the project's open question carried over from VIOT: it should dramatically raise local field emission risk even as its lower sputter yield reduces erosion — the same GNP trade-off VIOT's ion-optics testbed characterizes independently at the atomistic scale.

title: qsim-studio
description: A from-scratch, GPU-accelerated quantum computing simulator and visualization platform — statevectors, gates, measurement, and a circuit IR with QASM-2 support, built without external quantum libraries.

detail.tagline: A quantum computing simulator built from first principles — no Qiskit, no Cirq in the core — with a visualization layer for every milestone.
overview: qsim-studio is a local, GPU-accelerated quantum simulator built module by module against a public roadmap, with the explicit rule that external quantum frameworks (Qiskit, QuTiP) are only ever used inside an isolated validation layer to cross-check the from-scratch implementation — never inside the engine itself. Everything is pure Python plus NumPy/CuPy.

The build runs milestone-by-milestone: a quantum math engine (linear algebra, gates, single-qubit Bloch representation), a multi-qubit statevector register using tensor-contraction gate application, a measurement and statistics layer (Born-rule sampling, full/partial collapse, expectation values), and a circuit layer with its own intermediate representation, a QASM-2-subset parser/exporter, a gate-fusion optimizer, and an SVG circuit-diagram renderer.

resultsTable.caption: Roadmap milestones
rows: Linear algebra, gates, single-qubit Bloch sphere
Tensor-contraction gate application, Bell/GHZ states, entanglement entropy
Born sampling, collapse, expectation values, basis rotation
IR, QASM-2 subset, gate-fusion optimizer, SVG renderer

findings: Every milestone ships its own visualization: a Bloch sphere driven by real ⟨X⟩⟨Y⟩⟨Z⟩ expectation values, GHZ-state amplitude bars with entanglement entropy, an exact-vs-shot-noise measurement histogram showing convergence, and a circuit diagram rendered directly from the IR — not hand-drawn.

MP2's tensor-contraction statevector engine is cross-checked against a dense-matrix ground truth, and MP1's gate math includes oracle tests that activate automatically once Qiskit/QuTiP are installed, without becoming a hard dependency.
185 tests pass across the four completed milestones (24 + 36 + 52 + 73) with zero external quantum-library dependency in the core engine.

title: Rocket Nozzle Throat Insert — Microstructure-Informed FEA
description: Thermo-structural finite element analysis of a solid rocket motor nozzle throat insert: material selection (C-103), defect sensitivity, and microstructure-informed failure assessment.

detail.tagline: How big a manufacturing void can a rocket-nozzle throat insert tolerate at 1400°C before its factor of safety collapses to 1?
overview: A 10-phase ME301 course study (proposal → material selection → geometry → mesh → loads → baseline solve → defect sensitivity sweep → NDT mapping → microstructure writeup → final report) of a solid rocket motor nozzle throat insert. The material is locked to C-103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti), a BCC niobium alloy strengthened by solid-solution and precipitation hardening, chosen for retaining useful strength to roughly 1400°C — standard for rocket nozzle throats and re-entry leading edges.

The central engineering question is defect sensitivity: given that real castings and welds carry small voids, how does void size and depth-from-surface change the local stress-concentration factor and, ultimately, the factor of safety at operating temperature?

resultsTable.caption: Defect sensitivity sweep — stress concentration factor and factor of safety at 1400°C

chart.caption: Factor of safety vs. defect radius at 1400°C

dataset.label: 1400°C
dataset.value: Operating temperature evaluated for factor of safety

dataset.label: C-103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti)
dataset.value: Locked material — full property set in materials/

findings: The global stress field is dominated by the thermal gradient, not internal pressure — defect geometry only perturbs it locally.
Defect depth amplifies the stress-concentration factor non-linearly: the ratio of near-surface to mid-wall Kₜ grows from 1.00 at 0.2 mm radius to 1.35 at 2.0 mm.
A 2 mm near-surface void drives the factor of safety down to 1.29 at 1400°C — close enough to failure (FOS = 1) to be flagged as a critical defect class.

Practical implication carried into the NDT-mapping phase: near-surface voids larger than 1.5 mm within roughly a quarter wall-thickness of the bore must be reliably detectable by non-destructive testing before flight qualification.

title: ProfNet
description: A local-first personal CRM for academics — tracks professors, communications, reminders, and collaborations entirely on-device, with no cloud and no API keys.

detail.tagline: A CRM for research relationships — professors, correspondence, collaborations — that never leaves your machine.
overview: Academic outreach and collaboration tracking generates the same relationship-management problem as sales does — who did I contact, when, about what, and what's next — but existing CRMs assume a cloud backend and a company account. ProfNet is local-first by design: SQLite on disk via Prisma (WAL mode), file attachments in a local storage folder, no cloud services, and no API keys, packaged as both a web app and an Electron desktop app.

A `INVARIANTS.md` document specifies the data-integrity rules the app must never violate, enforced by a Vitest suite that runs directly over the server-action layer — so refactors that would silently corrupt data get caught before they ship.
findings: Both your database (`prisma/dev.db`) and file attachments (`./storage/`) are gitignored by design — none of your research contacts or notes ever leave your machine via git.
A one-click Settings → Download backup produces a zip of both paths; restoring is just unzipping over them and restarting the app.
Ships as a portable Electron build alongside the standard Next.js web app, using dnd-kit for drag-and-drop organization and shadcn/ui + Tailwind for the interface.

title: CFD Learning Series
description: A structured, beginner-to-intermediate CFD workflow in ANSYS Fluent — geometry through meshing, solving, and post-processing across three canonical cases of increasing complexity.

detail.tagline: The full CFD workflow — geometry, meshing, solving, post-processing — taught through three canonical cases of rising complexity.
overview: A self-structured learning project working through the standard CFD pipeline (Geometry → Meshing → Solver Setup → Solve → Post-Processing) in ANSYS Fluent, automated end-to-end with Fluent journal files (`.jou`) so every case is a one-command replay rather than a remembered sequence of GUI clicks.

Each case README pairs the physics background with step-by-step instructions, building from a simple steady solve to a genuinely unsteady one — the same progression a first CFD course follows, but self-paced and fully scripted.

resultsTable.caption: The three cases
rows: Velocity profiles, pressure drop vs. analytical solution
Vortex shedding, drag/lift monitors, transient setup

findings: Every case ships a Fluent journal file that automates the full TUI sequence — reading the mesh, setting physics, solving to convergence, and exporting results — so any case reruns identically with one command, headless or in the GUI.

The three-case progression is deliberately ordered by what changes: case 1 introduces the workflow on the simplest steady laminar solve, case 2 adds the unsteady vortex-shedding regime and force monitors, case 3 returns to steady but shifts focus to boundary-layer and entry-length behavior.

title: Sky Strike
description: A pixel-art retro plane shooter written as a single C file for native Windows — gamepad and keyboard input, zero game engine.

detail.tagline: A retro arcade shooter compiled from a single C file — no engine, no dependencies beyond the Win32 API.
overview: A pixel-art plane shooter built directly against Win32 (GDI for rendering, winmm for audio, dynamically-loaded XInput for gamepad support alongside keyboard controls), compiled with a single `gcc` invocation and no game engine.
findings: The project ships a working `sky_strike.exe` alongside its source — a `package.json` exists in the folder but is vestigial, since the game itself is pure C.
